# Scope and provenance

This notebook replaces unsupported conclusions in the historical exploratory report. Data describe Ames, Iowa. They do not validate valuation in Nicaragua. The original Rmd, HTML, Excel and XGBoost/blend experiments remain available as historical artifacts. See `docs/REVIEW_RESPONSE.md` for a verified response to the external review.

The revised experiment is a post hoc internal reassessment of a previously explored dataset. The inherited feature list is fixed before this new run, but cannot be presented as if no previous outcome-guided exploration had occurred.

```{r load}
source('R/revised_analysis.R')
if(!file.exists('reports/revised/holdout_metrics.csv')) source('run_analysis.R')
raw <- read_house_csv('data/raw/train.csv')
training_ids <- read.csv('reports/revised/split_ids.csv')
training_data <- raw[raw$Id %in% training_ids$Id[training_ids$partition=='training'],]
metrics <- read.csv('reports/revised/holdout_metrics.csv')
cv <- read.csv('reports/revised/cv_summary.csv')
coverage <- read.csv('reports/revised/interval_summary.csv')
config <- dget('reports/revised/run_config.R')
```

# Partition before preprocessing

A simple random 80/20 split uses seed 123: `r config$n_training` training houses and `r config$n_holdout` holdout houses. The split is performed on raw labeled data before learning medians, category mappings, scaling or rank filtering. Ten folds, balanced within log-price quartiles, are constructed in the training partition with seed 42. Each fold learns its own preprocessing and variance model. IDs for the split and folds are exported.

This differs from the original Rmd's stratified split and pre-split preprocessing. Scores from the two runs are not like-for-like estimates of an improvement caused by one isolated change.

```{r missingness}
missing <- sort(colSums(is.na(training_data)),decreasing=TRUE)
data.frame(variable=names(missing)[missing>0],missing=missing[missing>0])
```

The amount of missingness alone does not identify MAR/MNAR. Only basement-quality and garage-finish absence is labeled None in this corrected feature set. Other missing categorical values are Unknown. Numeric medians are learned from each fitting partition, not from the holdout or Kaggle test data.

# Feature engineering and a common design matrix

The original feature ideas are retained: sale year minus construction year, a porch-presence indicator from the four porch areas, full plus half-weighted bathrooms including basement, and indicators for pool, miscellaneous features, fireplaces and masonry. LotArea is logged; the response is log(SalePrice). OverallCond_grupo is now categorical, matching the original stated intention. Neighborhood, ExterQual, BsmtQual, KitchenQual and GarageFinish are retained.

Id, MoSold, redundant area components and the raw variables replaced by derived features are not predictors. Neighborhood categories below 0.5% (minimum two observations) are pooled; single-observation categories elsewhere are also handled using training-only mappings. If a rare pool has just one observation it falls back to the modal category, avoiding an isolated dummy with unit leverage. New categories map to the learned rare pool when available, otherwise to the training mode. These choices are explicit working encodings, not new fitted effects for unseen categories.

The same trained scaling, dummy columns and full-rank column subset are used for OLS and FGLS. Rank filtering is learned by QR decomposition in each training partition and held fixed when predicting. No `step_select(skip=TRUE)` remains in this corrected path.

```{r columns}
read.csv('reports/revised/model_features.csv')
```

# OLS and feasible GLS

With $z_i=\log(P_i)$, both models use the same mean design $z=X\beta+\epsilon$.

$$\widehat\beta_{OLS}=(X^TX)^{-1}X^Tz,\qquad
\widehat\beta_{WLS}=(X^TWX)^{-1}X^TWz.$$

The variance working model is fitted on training OLS residuals:

$$\log\{\max(e_i^2,\varepsilon)\}=\gamma_0+\gamma_1\widehat z_i+u_i,
\qquad w_i\propto\exp[-(\widehat\gamma_0+\widehat\gamma_1\widehat z_i)].$$

The small positive floor is computed from the training residuals. New-observation weights are predicted from that same variance model; they never use a new house's observed error. This is approximate FGLS, not a claim that the variance function is correctly specified or that weighting must improve prediction.

# Cross-validation and area sensitivity

Both policies are specified before assessment: fit all training houses, or fit only training houses with GrLivArea <4000. **All assessment and holdout houses remain in evaluation**. No response-, residual- or Cook-based row deletion is performed. This is a training-policy sensitivity analysis, not a blanket restriction to a smaller housing population.

```{r cv}
knitr::kable(cv,digits=5)
```

The model and training policy with the smallest mean CV RMSE in log price are used for the submission. The recorded choice is `r config$chosen_model` / `r config$chosen_policy`. Tiny differences between nearby CV means are descriptive and do not establish a statistically superior model. Test outcomes do not choose the policy or model.

# Holdout results

```{r performance}
knitr::kable(metrics,digits=5)
```

RMSE in log price is the primary metric. Dollar RMSE and MAE describe different losses. Predictive $R^2=1-SSE/SST$ is reported separately from squared Pearson correlation. Exponentiating a log prediction gives a median-type point prediction; it does not automatically estimate a conditional mean in dollars. No public Kaggle score is inferred from these holdout results.

# Diagnostics in the model's log scale

```{r diagnostics}
read.csv('reports/revised/diagnostics.csv')
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath('reports/revised/figures/log_residual_diagnostics.png'))
```

The auxiliary variance-association diagnostic regresses squared OLS log residuals on fitted log price and reports $nR^2$ against an asymptotic $\chi^2_1$ reference. Its p-value is diagnostic, not proof of homoscedasticity or causality. The Q-Q plot examines log-model residuals. A dollar-scale funnel is not by itself a violation of the log-error variance assumption; non-normal errors alone do not prove coefficient bias. Cook's distance is inspected on training rows without automatic deletion.

# Prediction intervals, not confidence intervals for the mean

For OLS on log price, an individual 95% interval is

$$\widehat z_0\pm t_{n-p,.975}\,s\sqrt{1+x_0^T(X^TX)^{-1}x_0}.$$

A mean-response confidence interval omits the future-error term 1. For the weighted fit, the working future variance is $s_w^2/w_0$, and coefficient uncertainty depends on $(X^TWX)^{-1}$. `predict.lm(..., interval='prediction', weights=w_new)` receives those predicted weights. This remains an approximate plug-in interval. Even a constant future-error variance does **not** imply constant total interval width because leverage varies with $x_0$.

Split conformal is a separate fixed OLS/all-properties baseline, independent of the CV winner. A fresh random split of the outer training data (seed 2026) uses `r config$n_proper` proper-training houses and `r config$n_calibration` calibration houses. The proper fit and preprocessing are not refitted after calibration. For $m$ calibration residual magnitudes $s_i=|z_i-\widehat z_i|$, use

$$k=\lceil(m+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil,\quad q=s_{(k)},\quad
[\exp(\widehat z_0-q),\exp(\widehat z_0+q)].$$

If $k>m$, the interval is unbounded; the code does not interpolate with R's default quantile type. The usual guarantee is marginal under exchangeability, not a 95% conditional guarantee for every house or a guarantee after geographic transfer. The conformal and full-training parametric intervals use different fitting sample sizes, which affects widths. Their area policies also differ, so the table does not isolate the effect of the interval method.

```{r intervals}
knitr::kable(coverage,digits=4)
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath('reports/revised/figures/interval_coverage.png'))
```

The binomial confidence limits describe uncertainty in the observed coverage fraction. A single coverage above 95% is insufficient to declare exact calibration or excessive population coverage. Consider coverage uncertainty together with interval width. Historical 98.98% WLS coverage and 96.01% in-sample Excel coverage remain archived and are not substituted for the new test assessment.

# Reproducibility and conclusions

Run `source('run_analysis.R')` from the repository root to regenerate CV, holdout results, intervals, figures, split/fold IDs and the revised submission. The core uses base R. `render_report.R` generates an HTML report without third-party packages. This notebook can optionally be knitted with rmarkdown/knitr.

The corrected results do not support the original claim of a large WLS gain or perfectly calibrated intervals. OLS and FGLS should be compared on shared features and validation partitions; their small empirical difference is retained rather than overstated. Original XGBoost/blend scripts have overlapping fit/evaluation data and are preserved as exploratory history, not included as verified revised competitors. A further common-validation XGBoost study would be a separate experiment.

The submission is generated only after assessment, using the CV-selected policy and model refitted on all labeled data. It has not been sent to Kaggle. The data remain specific to Ames, Iowa, and this internal reassessment does not establish geographic or temporal generalization.
